question: An admin needs to grant a team the ability to reset passwords for standard users but must not grant that team any other directory permissions. What is the best-practice approach?
options: Assign the built-in Helpdesk Administrator role, which is scoped for exactly this kind of limited password-reset task
Assign the Global Administrator role temporarily and remove it after the task is done
Create a custom role with only the microsoft.directory/users/password/update permission and assign it to the team
Add the team to the User Administrator role, which includes password reset among other user-management rights
explanation: A custom role scoped to only the password-update permission is the least-privilege choice. Helpdesk Administrator (A) is close but actually grants broader helpdesk permissions (including some support-ticket-style actions) beyond just password reset, so it's not the tightest scope. Global Administrator (B) is wildly overprivileged and manual removal is error-prone. User Administrator (D) includes full user lifecycle management, not just password reset, so it's broader than required.

question: Which statement about custom Microsoft Entra roles is accurate?
options: Custom roles can only be assigned at the tenant (directory) scope, never at a resource scope
Custom roles are built by combining specific resource-provider permissions and can be assigned at directory or administrative unit scope
Custom roles automatically inherit all permissions of the closest matching built-in role
Custom roles cannot be used to manage groups, only users
explanation: Custom Entra roles let you pick granular permissions and assign them at directory scope or narrower (like an administrative unit). They don't inherit from built-in roles (C is false — they're built permission-by-permission) and aren't restricted from group-management permissions (D is false) or limited to only tenant-wide scope (A is false, since AU scoping is a key feature).

question: A university wants its regional IT teams to manage users only within their own college (e.g., Engineering, Business) without seeing or managing users in other colleges. What Microsoft Entra feature best fits this requirement?
options: Dynamic security groups scoped by department attribute
Administrative units, with each college represented as its own unit and delegated admins scoped to it
Conditional Access policies targeting each department
Custom security attributes assigned to each user's department
explanation: Administrative units exist specifically to delegate scoped administration over a subset of users/groups/devices (like one college) without giving admins visibility into the rest of the directory. Dynamic groups (A) organize membership but don't scope admin permissions. Conditional Access (C) controls access policy, not admin delegation. Custom security attributes (D) are metadata/filtering tags, not a delegation boundary.

question: An administrator creates an administrative unit called 'EMEA Users' and adds a scoped role assignment of Helpdesk Administrator to a user for that unit. What is the effect?
options: The user can reset passwords for every user in the tenant, but the AU restricts their sign-in location to EMEA
The user's Helpdesk Administrator permissions apply only to members of the EMEA Users administrative unit, not the whole tenant
The AU assignment has no effect until the user is also given a tenant-wide role
Administrative units only support Global Administrator role assignments, so this configuration is invalid
explanation: Scoping a role assignment to an administrative unit restricts that role's effective permissions to just the members of that AU. It has nothing to do with sign-in location (A is a fabricated capability), doesn't require an additional tenant-wide role to function (C is false — the whole point of AU-scoped roles is that they work without one), and AUs support many roles beyond Global Administrator, in fact Global Administrator is typically NOT AU-scoped (D is false).

question: Which object types can be added as members of a Microsoft Entra administrative unit?
options: Users and groups only
Users, groups, and devices
Only security groups, not users directly
Only Microsoft 365 groups
explanation: Administrative units can contain users, groups, and devices, letting delegated admins manage all three object types within their scope. Restricting to just users and groups (A), only groups (C), or only M365 groups (D) all understate the supported membership types.

question: A user has been assigned the User Administrator role at the tenant level AND is also a member of an administrative unit where they hold the Helpdesk Administrator role. What best describes their effective permissions?
options: Only the more restrictive of the two roles applies
The two role assignments are additive — they have User Administrator's tenant-wide permissions plus Helpdesk Administrator's permissions scoped to the AU
Only the tenant-scoped assignment applies; the AU-scoped assignment is ignored
Their permissions default to Global Reader until an admin manually reconciles the conflict
explanation: Entra role assignments are additive — a user's effective permissions are the union of every assignment they hold, each respecting its own scope. There's no 'most restrictive wins' behavior (A is false), AU-scoped assignments aren't ignored (C is false), and there's no automatic downgrade to Global Reader (D is fabricated).

question: Which tool would an administrator use to check exactly which effective permissions a specific user has across role assignments before troubleshooting an access issue?
options: The 'Check access' / effective permissions view in Microsoft Entra ID for that user or role
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps risk score
The Azure Cost Management dashboard
Group naming policy settings
explanation: Microsoft Entra ID provides a way to view a user's effective role assignments (including inherited/scoped ones) so admins can audit exactly what access someone has. The other options (B, C, D) are unrelated services/features that don't surface role/permission data.

question: An organization wants to send email as user@contoso.com but their tenant's default domain is contoso.onmicrosoft.com. What must the admin do first before creating users with the contoso.com UPN suffix?
options: Nothing — any UPN suffix can be used immediately without verification
Add and verify the contoso.com custom domain in Microsoft Entra ID (e.g., via DNS TXT record) before it can be used as a UPN suffix
Purchase a Microsoft 365 Enterprise E5 license, which unlocks custom domains
Rename the default onmicrosoft.com domain to contoso.com
explanation: A custom domain must be added and verified (proving DNS ownership, typically via a TXT or MX record) before it becomes available as a UPN suffix or email domain option. Custom domains aren't gated by a specific license SKU (C is false) or usable without verification (A is false), and the onmicrosoft.com domain can't be renamed away, only supplemented (D is false).

question: What happens to a custom domain that becomes 'unverified' in Microsoft Entra ID (e.g., the DNS TXT record was removed)?
options: All users with that domain's UPN suffix are immediately deleted
The domain can no longer be used for new UPNs/email addresses and may eventually need re-verification; existing users generally keep functioning but the domain should be re-verified promptly
The tenant is automatically suspended by Microsoft
Nothing changes — verification is a one-time check with no ongoing relevance
explanation: An unverified domain risks losing its ability to be used for new configuration and should be re-verified, but Microsoft doesn't delete existing users (A is false) or suspend the tenant (C is false) over this. Verification isn't purely a one-time formality with zero ongoing relevance either (D is false) — losing verification is a real operational risk worth monitoring.

question: A company wants their sign-in page to show their logo and a custom background image instead of the default Microsoft branding. Where is this configured?
options: Company branding settings in Microsoft Entra ID
Conditional Access named locations
Microsoft Entra ID Protection policies
The tenant's custom domain DNS records
explanation: Company branding in Microsoft Entra ID lets admins customize the sign-in experience (logo, background image, layout, sign-in page text) per tenant and even per language/browser context. Conditional Access (B) and ID Protection (C) control access policy, not visual branding, and DNS records (D) have nothing to do with UI customization.

question: By default, can regular (non-admin) users in Microsoft Entra ID create new Microsoft 365 groups?
options: No, group creation is always restricted to Global Administrators only
Yes by default, but this can be restricted via tenant-level group settings to specific users or disabled entirely
No, only through PowerShell with elevated permissions can any group be created
Yes, but only security groups, never Microsoft 365 groups
explanation: Microsoft Entra ID ships with self-service group creation enabled for all users by default, but tenant-level group settings let admins restrict this to a designated set of users or turn it off. It's not locked to Global Admins only (A is false), not PowerShell-only (C is false), and the default behavior does include Microsoft 365 groups, not just security groups (D is false).

question: Which tenant-level setting controls whether users can register their own devices with Microsoft Entra ID?
options: Company branding settings
Device settings under Microsoft Entra ID, which include device registration and join policies
Conditional Access session controls
License assignment settings
explanation: Tenant-wide device settings govern device registration/join behavior, including which users are allowed to register devices and whether additional authentication (like MFA) is required to do so. Branding (A) is purely cosmetic, Conditional Access session controls (C) govern session behavior after sign-in rather than registration eligibility, and licensing (D) doesn't gate device registration policy.

question: An admin needs to create 50 new user accounts with a consistent naming convention and department attribute. What is the most efficient supported method?
options: Manually create each user one at a time through the Microsoft Entra admin center
Use a CSV bulk-create operation or a PowerShell script (Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK) to create all 50 users in one operation
Ask each of the 50 people to self-register their own accounts
Clone an existing user account 50 times
explanation: Bulk operations (CSV import in the admin center, or Microsoft Graph PowerShell scripting) are the supported, efficient way to create many users consistently. Manual one-by-one creation (A) doesn't scale well for 50 accounts, self-registration (C) isn't a standard admin-initiated provisioning method for employee accounts, and there's no 'clone a user' feature (D).

question: What is the effect of setting a user account's 'Block sign in' property to Yes?
options: The user's account and all data are permanently deleted
The user is temporarily prevented from signing in to any Microsoft Entra-connected service, but the account and its data remain intact
The user's licenses are automatically reassigned to another user
The user is added to a 'blocked users' security group visible to all admins
explanation: Blocking sign-in is a reversible way to disable access without deleting the account or its associated data/licenses. It doesn't delete anything (A is false), doesn't auto-reassign licenses (C is false — those stay assigned unless manually changed), and doesn't create any group membership (D is fabricated).

question: What is the key functional difference between a Microsoft 365 group and a security group in Microsoft Entra ID?
options: Security groups can only contain devices, never users

Microsoft 365 groups provide collaboration resources (shared mailbox, calendar, SharePoint site, Teams) in addition to access management, while security groups are purely for access/permission assignment
Security groups automatically sync to on-premises Active Directory while Microsoft 365 groups never do
Microsoft 365 groups cannot be used to assign application access
explanation: Microsoft 365 groups bundle collaboration resources on top of membership management; security groups exist solely to control access to resources/apps without those collaboration extras. Security groups aren't device-only (A is false), sync behavior isn't a defining difference and isn't described that way (C is false), and Microsoft 365 groups CAN be used for app assignment (D is false).

question: An admin wants group membership to automatically update based on a user attribute like department='Sales' with no manual maintenance. What should they configure?
options: An assigned (static) security group
A dynamic membership group with a rule based on the department attribute
A distribution list
A Conditional Access named location
explanation: Dynamic membership groups evaluate a rule (like user.department -eq "Sales") continuously and auto-update membership, exactly matching the no-manual-maintenance requirement. Assigned/static groups (A) require manual add/remove, distribution lists (C) are an Exchange-focused concept without Entra dynamic-rule support in this context, and named locations (D) are a Conditional Access network concept, unrelated to group membership.

question: What are custom security attributes in Microsoft Entra ID primarily used for?
options: Storing arbitrary business-defined attribute/value pairs on users or other objects, which can then be used for fine-grained authorization (e.g., in Conditional Access or RBAC conditions)
Encrypting a user's password before storage
Defining the visual theme of the sign-in page
Replacing the need for security groups entirely
explanation: Custom security attributes let organizations tag objects with their own key/value metadata (e.g., Project=Falcon, Classification=Confidential) for use in access decisions and reporting. They're unrelated to password encryption (B, which Microsoft always handles internally regardless), sign-in page branding (C), and they complement rather than replace security groups (D).

question: Which built-in role is specifically required to define new custom security attribute definitions (as opposed to just assigning existing attribute values to users)?
options: Any Global Administrator can always do this with no separate role needed
Attribute Definition Administrator (a distinct role from Attribute Assignment Administrator)
User Administrator
Helpdesk Administrator
explanation: Microsoft Entra deliberately splits this into two narrow roles: Attribute Definition Administrator can create/manage the attribute schema itself, while a separate Attribute Assignment Administrator role can only assign existing attribute values to objects — even Global Administrators do NOT get this by default without one of these roles (A is false), and User Administrator (C) / Helpdesk Administrator (D) don't include this capability.

question: An admin wants to reset the department attribute for 200 users listed in a CSV file. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Manually edit each of the 200 user profiles in the admin center UI
Write a Microsoft Graph PowerShell script that reads the CSV and calls Update-MgUser (or equivalent) in a loop for each user
Delete and recreate all 200 accounts with the new attribute
Use Company branding settings to apply the change tenant-wide
explanation: Scripting bulk attribute updates via Microsoft Graph PowerShell against a CSV input is the standard, efficient, and safe way to make the same kind of change across many accounts. Manual UI editing (A) doesn't scale to 200 users, deleting/recreating accounts (C) is destructive and unnecessary, and branding settings (D) have nothing to do with user attributes.

question: What must an administrator have installed and connected before running Microsoft Graph PowerShell cmdlets against a tenant?
options: Nothing — Microsoft Graph PowerShell cmdlets work without any module or authentication
The Microsoft.Graph PowerShell module, plus an authenticated connection (Connect-MgGraph) with appropriate delegated or application permissions/scopes
Only a valid Azure subscription, with no PowerShell module required
The legacy MSOnline module exclusively, since Microsoft Graph PowerShell doesn't support bulk operations
explanation: You need the Microsoft.Graph module installed and an authenticated session (Connect-MgGraph) requesting the right Graph API permission scopes for whatever objects/actions the script performs. PowerShell can't run without a module and auth (A is false), an Azure subscription alone isn't what authorizes Graph calls (C is false), and Microsoft Graph PowerShell fully supports bulk-style scripted operations, making the claim in D false.

question: What is the difference between a Microsoft Entra joined device and a Microsoft Entra registered device?
options: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable

A joined device is fully owned/managed by the organization with an org-issued Entra identity as its primary account; a registered device is typically a personal/BYOD device that just has an Entra identity added alongside its existing local/personal account
Registered devices support Conditional Access, but joined devices do not
Joined devices are only for mobile phones, while registered devices are only for desktops
explanation: Entra join is meant for corporate-owned devices with the org identity as the primary sign-in account; Entra registration (e.g., via 'Add work or school account') is meant for BYOD scenarios where the device keeps its personal primary account. There absolutely is a meaningful difference (A is false), both joined and registered devices can be Conditional Access targets (C is false), and neither is restricted by device form factor the way D claims.

question: An admin removes a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license from a user who currently has active Conditional Access and Identity Protection policies applying to them. What is the most likely effect?
options: Nothing changes, licenses have no bearing on which policies apply
P2-dependent features (like Identity Protection risk-based policies) stop being enforced for that user once the license is removed, since those features require an active P2 (or equivalent) license
The user's account is automatically deleted
The removal is blocked by Entra ID until all policies referencing the user are deleted first
explanation: Premium features like Identity Protection and certain Conditional Access risk-based controls require an assigned P2 (or bundled equivalent) license per user; removing it typically stops those specific premium capabilities from applying to that user going forward. License changes don't delete accounts (C is false) or get blocked by pending policy references (D is false), and licensing absolutely does affect feature availability, so A is false.

question: What is 'group-based licensing' used for in Microsoft Entra ID?
options: Automatically assigning (and removing) licenses to users based on their membership in a group, rather than assigning licenses to each user individually
Restricting which groups can be created based on license SKU
Encrypting group membership data
Preventing dynamic groups from being created
explanation: Group-based licensing assigns a license SKU to a group; any user added to that group inherits the license automatically, and it's removed if they leave — a major administrative time-saver over per-user assignment. The other options describe capabilities that don't exist or aren't what group-based licensing does.

question: An organization wants to restrict which external domains its employees can invite as B2B guest users (e.g., only trusted partner domains). Where is this configured?
options: External collaboration settings in Microsoft Entra ID, using the allowlist/denylist for collaboration domains
Conditional Access named locations
Company branding settings
Custom security attribute definitions
explanation: External collaboration settings include domain allow/deny lists that govern which external domains employees can invite as B2B guests. Named locations (B) are a network-location concept for Conditional Access, unrelated to invite domain restrictions; branding (C) and security attributes (D) have no bearing on this.

question: What is the most efficient way to invite 30 external partners as B2B guest users at once?
options: Send each partner a personal email asking them to self-register an account
Use the bulk invite feature (CSV upload) in Microsoft Entra ID to invite all 30 at once
Individually create each guest invitation through the UI one at a time
Ask the partners' own IT department to create the accounts in your tenant
explanation: Microsoft Entra ID supports a bulk invite (CSV-based) flow specifically for inviting many external users at once. Ad hoc email requests (A) aren't a formal provisioning method, one-by-one UI invitations (C) don't scale efficiently to 30 people, and another organization's IT team cannot create accounts inside your tenant (D).

question: A B2B guest user's access needs to be reviewed and removed if they no longer need it. What Entra capability directly supports periodically checking and removing stale guest access?
options: Access reviews
Company branding settings
Custom domains
Device join settings
explanation: Access reviews (part of identity governance) are designed exactly for periodically validating whether guest (or any) access should continue, with reviewers able to approve or remove access. Branding (B), custom domains (C), and device join settings (D) are unrelated to reviewing or revoking external user access.

question: What do Cross-tenant access settings in Microsoft Entra ID primarily control?
options: How your organization's users collaborate with (and are trusted by) specific other Microsoft Entra tenants, including inbound and outbound trust settings for MFA and device compliance claims
The DNS settings for your tenant's custom domains
Which licenses are available for purchase
The visual theme of the admin portal
explanation: Cross-tenant access settings define organization-specific (or default) trust relationships with other Entra tenants — for example, trusting another tenant's MFA claim so your users aren't prompted again, and controlling B2B/B2B-direct-connect collaboration inbound/outbound. DNS (B), licensing (C), and portal theming (D) are unrelated capabilities.

question: An organization wants to trust a partner tenant's multifactor authentication so their users aren't prompted for MFA again when accessing shared resources. What should be configured?
options: A Conditional Access named location for the partner's IP range
An inbound cross-tenant access setting trusting the partner tenant's MFA claim
A custom security attribute on each partner user
Company branding matching the partner's logo
explanation: Trusting another tenant's MFA claim is done through cross-tenant access settings (inbound trust settings), which is the mechanism designed for this exact scenario. A named location (A) only addresses network location, not MFA trust; custom attributes (C) and branding (D) don't affect authentication trust between tenants.

question: What is the purpose of cross-tenant synchronization in Microsoft Entra ID?
options: Automatically provisioning and keeping user accounts synchronized from a source tenant into one or more target tenants, commonly used across multiple tenants within the same larger organization (e.g., after a merger)
Synchronizing on-premises Active Directory with a single Entra tenant
Backing up all tenant configuration to Azure Blob Storage
Synchronizing Conditional Access policies between test and production tenants
explanation: Cross-tenant synchronization automates user provisioning/deprovisioning between separate Entra tenants that belong to the same overall organization (common post-M&A or multi-subsidiary scenario). On-prem AD sync to a single tenant (B) describes Entra Connect Sync/Cloud Sync instead, and there's no built-in feature matching C or D as described.

question: An organization needs to let users from a partner company sign in using the partner's own SAML-based identity provider, without creating separate Entra accounts for each partner user. What should be configured?
options: A dynamic security group for the partner's users
A federated (SAML/WS-Fed) external identity provider connection in External Identities
A custom security attribute mapping
Group-based licensing for the partner domain
explanation: External Identities supports configuring federation with an external SAML or WS-Fed identity provider so users authenticate with their home IdP without needing locally-managed Entra credentials. A dynamic group (A) only affects membership rules, not authentication federation, and C/D don't relate to identity provider federation at all.

question: What is the primary purpose of Microsoft Entra Connect Sync?
options: Synchronizing identity objects (users, groups, contacts) and their attributes from an on-premises Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID
Providing single sign-on for SaaS apps with no on-premises component
Managing Conditional Access policies across multiple tenants
Encrypting data at rest in Azure Storage
explanation: Entra Connect Sync (the successor to Azure AD Connect) is the on-premises-to-cloud directory synchronization engine, keeping hybrid identity objects and attributes consistent. SSO for pure-cloud SaaS apps without an on-prem component (B) isn't its purpose, and it has nothing to do with cross-tenant Conditional Access management (C) or storage encryption (D).

question: An organization wants only users in a specific OU to sync to Microsoft Entra ID, excluding all others. What Entra Connect Sync feature enables this?
options: Password hash synchronization
Scoping filters (OU-based filtering) configured during or after Connect Sync setup
Seamless SSO
Pass-through authentication
explanation: Entra Connect Sync supports OU-based (and attribute-based) scoping filters so only selected on-prem objects sync to the cloud. Password hash sync (A), seamless SSO (C), and pass-through authentication (D) are all authentication-method features, not object-scoping/filtering features.

question: How does Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync differ from Entra Connect Sync in terms of architecture?
options: There is no architectural difference, they are the same product with different names

Cloud Sync uses lightweight, cloud-managed provisioning agents (with agent auto-update and simpler multi-forest support) instead of the single, locally-installed and locally-managed Connect Sync server
Cloud Sync only supports Conditional Access, not user provisioning
Cloud Sync requires disabling all on-premises Active Directory
explanation: Cloud Sync uses lightweight provisioning agents managed from the cloud, simplifying multi-forest scenarios and reducing on-prem management overhead compared to the traditional Connect Sync server model. They are meaningfully different products (A is false), Cloud Sync's core purpose IS user provisioning (C is false), and it doesn't require disabling on-prem AD (D is false — it still reads from AD, just via lightweight agents).

question: What does password hash synchronization actually synchronize to Microsoft Entra ID?
options: The user's plaintext password
A hash of the password hash (a further-hashed representation), never the reversible plaintext or the raw on-prem hash
Only the password's length and complexity score
Nothing password-related; only the account's existence syncs
explanation: Password hash sync takes the on-prem password hash and hashes it again (using a per-user salt) before sending it to Entra ID — the plaintext password is never transmitted or stored in the cloud. Options A, C, and D all misdescribe what's actually synchronized.

question: With pass-through authentication (PTA) enabled, where does the actual password validation occur during sign-in?
options: Entirely in the cloud, using a synchronized password hash
On-premises, validated directly against Active Directory Domain Services via a lightweight PTA agent, with no password hash stored in the cloud
On the user's local device only
Validation is skipped entirely if PTA is enabled
explanation: PTA forwards the authentication request through a lightweight on-prem agent that validates the password directly against AD DS in real time — no password hash is stored in Entra ID for PTA users. This is the key distinction from password hash sync (A describes PHS, not PTA), and validation isn't purely local-device (C) or skipped (D).

question: What problem does Seamless Single Sign-On (SSO) solve for hybrid identity users on a domain-joined, on-prem network?
options: It eliminates the need for any authentication method (password hash sync or PTA) entirely
It automatically signs users in to Microsoft Entra ID resources when they're already signed in to their domain-joined corporate device, avoiding a repeated password prompt
It replaces Conditional Access policies
It only works for cloud-only (non-hybrid) accounts
explanation: Seamless SSO works alongside password hash sync or PTA to silently authenticate users already signed in to a domain-joined device, avoiding redundant credential prompts on the corporate network — it doesn't remove the need for an underlying auth method (A is false), doesn't replace Conditional Access (C is false), and it's specifically a hybrid-identity feature, not for cloud-only accounts (D is false).

question: An organization currently uses AD FS for federated sign-in and wants to reduce on-premises infrastructure dependency by moving to a cloud-managed authentication method. Which migration path is most appropriate?
options: Migrate to password hash synchronization or pass-through authentication (with Seamless SSO), retiring the AD FS federation servers
Migrate to Conditional Access named locations
Migrate all users to guest (B2B) accounts
There is no supported migration path away from AD FS
explanation: Microsoft explicitly supports and documents migrating AD FS federation to password hash sync or pass-through authentication (paired with Seamless SSO), reducing the on-prem footprint. Named locations (B) are unrelated to authentication method migration, converting users to guests (C) would be a fundamentally different and inappropriate change, and a supported path absolutely exists, making D false.

question: What is the primary function of Microsoft Entra Connect Health?
options: Monitoring the health, performance, and reliability of on-premises hybrid identity infrastructure components (like Connect Sync servers, AD FS servers, and domain controllers) with alerts
Encrypting synchronized password hashes
Managing license assignment for hybrid users
Providing a chat-based support agent for identity issues
explanation: Connect Health provides monitoring, alerting, and usage analytics for hybrid identity infrastructure (sync servers, AD FS, domain controllers), helping admins catch issues like sync failures or AD FS downtime proactively. It isn't an encryption feature (B), licensing tool (C), or support chat product (D).

question: An admin notices Connect Health alerts showing repeated sync errors for a subset of on-prem AD objects. What is the most likely underlying cause category these alerts help surface?
options: Attribute conflicts, duplicate attribute values (e.g., duplicate UPN or proxyAddress), or objects violating Entra ID's schema/validation rules during sync
A billing issue with the Azure subscription
An expired SSL certificate on the tenant's custom domain's website
A misconfigured Conditional Access policy
explanation: Connect Health sync error alerts most commonly point to data-quality issues on the on-prem side — duplicate or invalid attribute values that fail Entra ID's validation during sync. Billing (B), an unrelated website certificate (C), and Conditional Access policy misconfiguration (D) are not what sync-error alerts are diagnosing.

question: Which statement about configuring external identity providers for federation (SAML/WS-Fed) in Microsoft Entra External ID is accurate?
options: Federation requires manually recreating every partner user as a local Entra account first
Federation lets users authenticate with their home organization's IdP credentials directly, with Entra trusting SAML/WS-Fed assertions from the configured external IdP
Only WS-Fed is supported; SAML federation is not available
Federated external IdPs can only be used for guest access to SharePoint, no other apps
explanation: Configuring an external SAML/WS-Fed IdP establishes trust so Entra accepts assertions from that IdP directly — no local account duplication is required (A is false), both SAML and WS-Fed are supported protocols (C is false), and federated access isn't restricted to SharePoint-only scenarios (D is false).

question: When planning an authentication strategy for a mixed workforce (some fully remote, some in secure offices with managed devices), what is the most important first step?
options: Immediately enable every available authentication method for every user
Inventory user populations, their device/network context, and risk tolerance, then map appropriate authentication methods and MFA requirements to each population
Disable all legacy authentication methods before assessing user needs
Purchase the highest-tier license SKU for all users regardless of role
explanation: Good authentication planning starts with understanding who your users are, how/where they work, and the risk each population represents, then tailoring methods and policies accordingly. Enabling everything indiscriminately (A) creates confusion and unnecessary support burden, disabling legacy auth before understanding usage (C) could break things without assessment, and blanket licensing (D) doesn't address the actual planning question.

question: An organization wants smart-card-equivalent strong authentication for users without deploying physical smart cards. Which Microsoft Entra authentication method is designed for this?
options: Self-service password reset
Certificate-based authentication (CBA), using X.509 certificates issued to users' devices
Company branding
Group-based licensing
explanation: Certificate-based authentication lets Entra ID validate X.509 client certificates directly (cloud-native, no on-prem federation server required) as a phishing-resistant primary or MFA factor. SSPR (A), branding (C), and licensing (D) have nothing to do with certificate-based strong authentication.

question: A new hire needs to bootstrap Microsoft Authenticator and complete initial sign-in before they have any registered authentication methods. What feature is designed for exactly this scenario?
options: Temporary Access Pass (TAP), a time-limited passcode an admin issues for initial or recovery sign-in
Self-service password reset
Windows Hello for Business
Passkeys (FIDO2)
explanation: Temporary Access Pass is built for bootstrapping — a time-limited, admin-issued code that lets a user sign in and register their permanent authentication methods without already having one. SSPR (B) requires an existing method to verify identity first, Windows Hello (C) and passkeys (D) are end-state strong methods, not bootstrap mechanisms.

question: In the context of Microsoft Entra ID authentication methods, what role do OAuth 2.0 tokens (access tokens, refresh tokens) play?
options: They are used exclusively for password reset flows
They represent the credentials/proof of authentication and authorization that client apps present to access protected resources after a user or service successfully authenticates
They are a type of MFA hardware token
They replace the need for Conditional Access entirely
explanation: OAuth 2.0 tokens are the artifacts issued after successful auth/consent that apps use to call APIs on the user's or app's behalf — they're a core part of the modern auth flow, not a password-reset mechanism (A), physical hardware (C), or a Conditional Access replacement (D).

question: Which of the following is NOT a capability of the Microsoft Authenticator app in an Entra ID authentication context?
options: Push notification approval for MFA
Passwordless phone sign-in
Number matching to reduce MFA fatigue/prompt-bombing attacks
Automatically provisioning new user accounts in bulk
explanation: Microsoft Authenticator handles push-based MFA approval, passwordless phone sign-in, and number matching (a defense against MFA fatigue attacks) — all real capabilities (A, B, C). Bulk account provisioning (D) is an admin/directory management function, not something the Authenticator app does.

question: What security property makes passkeys (FIDO2) phishing-resistant compared to a password or SMS one-time code?
options: Passkeys use a longer numeric code than SMS
Passkeys are cryptographically bound to the specific website/relying party they were registered for, so they cannot be entered on a lookalike phishing site
Passkeys require a VPN connection to function
Passkeys expire after 24 hours, unlike passwords
explanation: FIDO2/passkey authentication is origin-bound — the cryptographic challenge-response only works against the legitimate relying party domain, so a phishing site simply can't complete the handshake even if a user is tricked into visiting it. Code length (A), VPN requirement (C), and expiration timing (D) aren't what makes passkeys phishing-resistant.

question: Where would an admin configure which MFA methods (e.g., Authenticator push, SMS, voice call) are available tenant-wide for users to register?
options: Authentication methods policy in Microsoft Entra ID
Company branding settings
Administrative units
Custom security attribute definitions
explanation: The Authentication methods policy is the tenant-wide control surface for enabling/disabling and scoping which MFA/authentication methods users are allowed to register and use. Branding (B), administrative units (C), and custom attributes (D) don't govern which auth methods are available.

question: What is a prerequisite for a user to be able to successfully use self-service password reset (SSPR)?
options: The user must have Global Administrator rights
SSPR must be enabled for the user (or their group) at the tenant level, and the user must have registered the required number of authentication methods for reset
The user's device must be Microsoft Entra joined
The organization must be using AD FS
explanation: SSPR requires tenant-level enablement (targeting specific users/groups or all users) plus the user having registered enough verified methods to meet the configured combined registration requirement. It has nothing to do with admin rights (A), device join state (C), or AD FS (D — SSPR works independent of federation choice, though writeback to on-prem AD is a separate related setting).

question: A hybrid organization wants a password reset performed via Entra SSPR to also update the user's on-premises Active Directory password. What must be enabled?
options: SSPR writeback (password writeback) to on-premises Active Directory, typically via Entra Connect Sync or Cloud Sync
Nothing extra — SSPR automatically updates on-prem AD
Seamless SSO
Company branding
explanation: Password writeback is a distinct, explicitly-enabled feature that pushes an SSPR-driven password change back down to on-prem AD via the sync engine — it doesn't happen automatically without enabling it (B is false), and it's unrelated to Seamless SSO (C) or branding (D).

question: What authentication factor does Windows Hello for Business primarily rely on?
options: A shared secret transmitted over the network at every sign-in, similar to a traditional password
A cryptographic key pair bound to the specific device, unlocked locally by a PIN or biometric (never transmitted over the network)
A physical smart card that must be inserted at every sign-in
An SMS code sent to the user's registered phone
explanation: Windows Hello for Business provisions an asymmetric key pair tied to the device's TPM; the private key is unlocked locally via PIN/biometric and never leaves the device or crosses the network, unlike a shared-secret password (A). It doesn't require a physical smart card insertion (C) and isn't SMS-based (D).

question: An employee is terminated immediately. Blocking their sign-in alone may not be enough because they already have active, unexpired sessions/tokens on multiple devices. What additional action should the admin take?
options: Nothing further is needed once sign-in is blocked
Revoke the user's active refresh tokens/sessions (e.g., via 'Revoke sessions' or Continuous Access Evaluation-triggered revocation) so already-issued tokens stop working promptly
Delete the user's mailbox only
Change the tenant's default domain
explanation: Blocking future sign-in doesn't invalidate tokens already issued to active sessions; explicitly revoking sessions/refresh tokens is necessary to cut off access from devices that are already signed in. Deleting only the mailbox (C) doesn't address directory/app session access, and changing the default domain (D) is unrelated and disruptive.

question: What does Microsoft Entra Password Protection primarily do?
options: Encrypts all stored passwords with a stronger algorithm

Blocks users from setting passwords that match a global Microsoft banned-password list plus a customizable organization-specific banned list (and can extend enforcement to on-premises AD via a proxy/DC agent)
Automatically resets any password older than 90 days
Provides passwordless sign-in for all users automatically
explanation: Password Protection checks new/changed passwords against Microsoft's global banned list and a custom organization list (like company name variations), rejecting weak or predictable choices, and can be extended on-premises via the Password Protection Proxy and DC agent. It's not about encryption algorithm changes (A), automatic expiry-based resets (C), or blanket passwordless enablement (D).

question: What problem does Microsoft Entra Kerberos solve for hybrid identity organizations that have moved away from AD FS or PTA/PHS-only authentication?
options: It replaces the need for on-premises Active Directory entirely

It allows Microsoft Entra ID to issue Kerberos service tickets (via a special Entra Kerberos computer object) so hybrid users can access on-premises resources that require Kerberos (like file shares) using cloud-driven authentication such as Windows Hello for Business
It is used only for encrypting SharePoint Online documents
It removes the need for any authentication method registration
explanation: Entra Kerberos bridges cloud-based authentication (e.g., Windows Hello for Business) to on-prem Kerberos-dependent resources by letting Entra ID issue valid Kerberos tickets via a dedicated computer object in AD — it doesn't eliminate on-prem AD (A is false), isn't a SharePoint-specific encryption feature (C), and doesn't remove registration requirements (D).

question: When planning Conditional Access policies, what is the recommended approach to avoid accidentally locking all admins out of the tenant?
options: Enable 'block all access' policies immediately in enforced mode for every user including admins
Use report-only mode to test policy impact first, and always exclude at least one break-glass/emergency access account from restrictive policies
Never use Conditional Access for admin accounts
Apply Conditional Access only to guest users, never to employees
explanation: Best practice is to validate policies in report-only mode before enforcing, and to maintain excluded break-glass accounts so a policy misconfiguration can't lock out all administrative access. Immediately enforcing block-all policies (A) is how lockouts happen, entirely exempting admins from Conditional Access (C) creates a security gap, and restricting CA to guests only (D) ignores the much larger population of regular users needing protection.

question: In a Conditional Access policy, what does the 'Assignments' section define?
options: Which controls (block, grant with MFA, etc.) are applied
The scope of who and what the policy applies to — users/groups, cloud apps or actions, and conditions like device platform, location, or sign-in risk
The billing account charged for the policy
The custom branding shown during sign-in
explanation: Assignments define the WHO/WHAT/WHEN scope of a policy (target users/groups, target apps, and conditions), separate from the Access Controls section which defines the resulting grant/block/session actions. Billing (C) and branding (D) are unrelated to CA policy structure.

question: A Conditional Access policy is configured with grant controls requiring 'Require multifactor authentication' AND 'Require compliant device', with the control-combination logic set to 'Require all the selected controls'. What must a user satisfy to be granted access?
options: Either MFA or a compliant device, whichever is easier
Both MFA AND a compliant device must be satisfied
Neither is actually enforced unless a third control is also added
Only a compliant device; MFA is ignored when device compliance is also selected
explanation: When grant controls are combined with 'require all', every selected control must be individually satisfied — access isn't granted with just one satisfied (A is false), the controls are enforced as configured without needing a third (C is false), and MFA is not silently ignored (D is false).

question: An admin wants to see which Conditional Access policies would have applied to a hypothetical sign-in (specific user, app, location) without actually enforcing anything yet. What tool should they use?
options: The 'What If' tool in Conditional Access
Company branding preview
Access reviews simulation
PIM audit history
explanation: The Conditional Access 'What If' tool simulates policy evaluation for a given set of sign-in conditions, showing which policies would apply, without requiring an actual sign-in or report-only enforcement. Branding preview (B), access review simulation (C), and PIM audit history (D) don't provide this kind of hypothetical CA evaluation.

question: After enabling a new Conditional Access policy, several users report unexpected sign-in blocks. What is the best first troubleshooting step?
options: Immediately delete the policy without investigation
Review the Sign-in logs for the affected users, checking which Conditional Access policies applied and why access was denied (the 'Conditional Access' tab on the sign-in event)
Reset the affected users' passwords
Disable Conditional Access for the entire tenant
explanation: Sign-in logs show exactly which policies evaluated to what result for a specific sign-in attempt, making them the fastest way to diagnose an unexpected block. Deleting the policy outright (A) or disabling CA tenant-wide (D) are overcorrections that remove protection without understanding the cause, and resetting passwords (C) doesn't address a policy-evaluation issue.

question: Which Conditional Access session control would force a user to re-authenticate periodically during a long browser session, even if their token would otherwise still be valid?
options: Sign-in frequency
Company branding
Custom security attributes
Password protection
explanation: Sign-in frequency is a session control that forces re-authentication after a configured time period, overriding the default token lifetime behavior. Branding (B), custom attributes (C), and password protection (D) are unrelated session controls.

question: An organization wants to block access to a sensitive app from any device that is not marked compliant in Intune, regardless of user identity risk. What Conditional Access approach fits?
options: A grant control requiring 'Require device to be marked as compliant', targeting the sensitive app
A sign-in risk policy in ID Protection only
A session control limiting file download only
A named location restricting by country
explanation: Requiring the device-compliance grant control directly enforces the 'must be Intune-compliant' requirement for the targeted app, independent of user risk signals. A pure sign-in risk policy (B) evaluates risk, not device compliance; download restriction (C) and country-based named locations (D) don't address the compliance requirement described.

question: What problem does Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) address compared to traditional token-lifetime-based access control?
options: It makes access tokens last indefinitely so users never have to sign in again
It enables near-real-time revocation of access (e.g., when a user is disabled, password changed, or high sign-in risk detected) instead of waiting for the access token to naturally expire
It replaces Conditional Access policies entirely
It only applies to on-premises applications
explanation: CAE-enabled services/apps receive near-real-time signals (like account disablement, password reset, or detected risk) and can revoke access immediately rather than waiting up to the token's full lifetime to expire — it doesn't make tokens last forever (A is false, that's the opposite goal), doesn't replace Conditional Access (C — it complements it), and specifically targets cloud-connected CAE-aware services, not classic on-prem-only apps (D).

question: An organization wants to require step-up MFA only when a user tries to open a specific highly sensitive SharePoint document library, not for general SharePoint access. What Conditional Access feature enables this granular, action-specific targeting?
options: Named locations
Authentication context, tagged on the sensitive resource (e.g., via a sensitivity label) and referenced in a targeted Conditional Access policy
Company branding
Custom security attribute definitions
explanation: Authentication context lets you define specific 'auth context' tags that can be attached to sensitive resources/actions (like a sensitivity label on a document library) and then targeted with their own Conditional Access policy — providing far more granularity than app-wide policies. Named locations (A) address network location, not resource sensitivity, and branding (C) / custom attributes (D) don't provide this targeting mechanism.

question: What are 'protected actions' in the context of Microsoft Entra Conditional Access?
options: A list of blocked IP addresses

Specific high-impact administrative permissions/tasks (like updating Conditional Access policies themselves or federation settings) that can require additional Conditional Access enforcement (like step-up authentication) before they can be performed
A category of licensed apps only available to E5 tenants
A synonym for access reviews
explanation: Protected actions let admins require extra Conditional Access enforcement (e.g., phishing-resistant MFA) before a sensitive administrative action can be performed, adding a safeguard against a compromised admin session being used to weaken security controls. It's not an IP blocklist (A), an app-licensing category (C), or the same thing as access reviews (D).

question: What is the benefit of creating a Conditional Access policy from a Microsoft-provided template rather than building one entirely from scratch?
options: Templates automatically enforce the policy in production with no review needed

Templates provide a pre-built, Microsoft-recommended baseline configuration (e.g., 'Require MFA for admins') that an admin can review, customize, and then enable — reducing setup time and the chance of missing a best-practice control
Templates can only be used by Global Administrators and no one else
Templates remove the need for any user or group assignment
explanation: CA policy templates give a vetted starting point aligned to common best-practice scenarios, which admins still review/customize before enabling — they aren't auto-enforced without review (A is false), aren't restricted to only Global Administrators among eligible CA-capable roles (C is an overstatement), and still require normal assignment configuration (D is false).

question: Microsoft Entra ID Protection flags a user as 'high user risk' due to leaked credentials found in a known breach. What is an appropriate policy response using ID Protection or Conditional Access?
options: Ignore the flag since leaked credential detections are usually false positives
Require the user to securely change their password (self-remediation) or block access until an admin resolves it, via a user risk-based Conditional Access policy
Immediately and permanently delete the user's account
Disable Conditional Access for that user going forward
explanation: A user-risk policy can require secure password change as self-remediation (or block access pending investigation) when leaked-credential risk is detected — this is a real, high-confidence signal, not something to dismiss (A is false). Permanent deletion (C) is a wildly disproportionate response, and disabling Conditional Access for a risky user (D) is the opposite of an appropriate response.

question: What distinguishes 'sign-in risk' from 'user risk' in Microsoft Entra ID Protection?
options: They are the same signal, just named differently in different portals

Sign-in risk evaluates the likelihood that a specific sign-in attempt is not the legitimate user (e.g., unfamiliar location, anonymized IP, impossible travel); user risk evaluates the probability that the user's identity itself has been compromised (e.g., leaked credentials), aggregated across the account over time
User risk only applies to guest accounts
Sign-in risk can only be evaluated for hybrid identities
explanation: Sign-in risk is a per-sign-in-event evaluation (real-time signals like impossible travel or anonymized IP), while user risk is an account-level, longer-horizon assessment (like confirmed leaked credentials) — they're distinct signals feeding different but related risk policies. They aren't the same thing under different names (A is false), user risk isn't guest-only (C is false), and sign-in risk isn't limited to hybrid identities (D is false).

question: An admin wants to proactively nudge users who haven't yet registered Microsoft Authenticator to do so, without forcing an abrupt requirement change. What Entra ID feature is designed for this?
options: Authentication methods registration campaign, which prompts eligible users to set up a stronger method (like Authenticator) during sign-in over time
Immediately deleting their account if not registered within 24 hours
Company branding change
Access reviews targeting registration status
explanation: Registration campaigns are purpose-built to nudge users toward registering a specific stronger authentication method during normal sign-in, gradually improving MFA coverage. Account deletion (B) is a wildly disproportionate non-feature, branding (C) is cosmetic, and access reviews (D) govern access grants, not method registration nudging.

question: Where would an administrator go to see a consolidated, filterable list of currently flagged risky users and risky sign-ins for investigation?
options: The Risky users and Risky sign-ins reports in Microsoft Entra ID Protection
Company branding settings
License assignment reports
Administrative unit membership list
explanation: ID Protection's Risky users and Risky sign-ins reports are the dedicated views for reviewing, filtering, and acting on detected risk (confirm compromised, dismiss, remediate). None of the other options (branding, license reports, AU membership) surface risk detection data.

question: An investigation confirms a flagged 'risky user' was genuinely compromised. What is the recommended remediation sequence?
options: Do nothing further since the risk was already flagged automatically
Confirm the user as compromised in ID Protection, force a secure password reset/revoke sessions, and investigate for further impact (e.g., mailbox rules, OAuth app consents granted by the attacker)
Immediately delete the user's account with no investigation of downstream impact
Only change the user's display name
explanation: Proper remediation includes confirming the compromise (which trains the risk model), forcing credential reset and session revocation, and checking for attacker persistence mechanisms like malicious inbox rules or rogue app consents — doing nothing (A) leaves the account exposed, outright deletion without investigation (C) can destroy forensic evidence and disrupt business continuity unnecessarily, and a display name change (D) does nothing for security.

question: Microsoft Entra ID Protection can also flag risk for workload identities (service principals/apps), not just human users. What kind of signal commonly triggers a workload identity risk detection?
options: The service principal's client secret or certificate being used from an unfamiliar location or leaked in a public code repository
The workload identity's display name being changed
The workload identity being assigned a new custom security attribute
The workload identity's Company branding logo changing
explanation: Workload identity risk detections focus on anomalous credential usage patterns — like sign-ins from atypical locations or credentials found exposed in public repos — which indicate the app's credentials may be compromised. Display name changes (B), custom attribute assignment (C), and branding (D) aren't risk signals for workload identities.

question: What is the Global Secure Access Client used for?
options: It's the endpoint agent installed on user devices that routes traffic to Microsoft's Security Service Edge (SSE) so Global Secure Access policies (Private Access, Internet Access) can be enforced
It is a server-side proxy installed only in Azure
It replaces the need for Conditional Access
It is a licensing management tool
explanation: The Global Secure Access Client is the device-side agent that forwards relevant traffic into Microsoft's Security Service Edge so Global Secure Access policies can inspect and enforce identity-aware network access — it's not a server-only proxy (B), doesn't replace Conditional Access (C, which it actually integrates with), and isn't a licensing tool (D).

question: What does Microsoft Entra Private Access (part of Global Secure Access) primarily provide?
options: Identity-aware, Zero Trust access to private/on-premises applications and resources without requiring a traditional full-tunnel VPN
Antivirus scanning for email attachments
Company branding for the sign-in page
License assignment automation
explanation: Private Access delivers Zero Trust Network Access to internal/private resources (replacing traditional VPN-style broad network access) with identity- and Conditional-Access-aware per-app access. It has nothing to do with antivirus scanning (B), branding (C), or license automation (D).

question: What is the primary purpose of Microsoft Entra Internet Access (part of Global Secure Access)?
options: Providing a Secure Web Gateway (SWG) that applies identity-aware security policies to general internet-bound and SaaS traffic
Managing on-premises Active Directory replication
Configuring custom domains for the tenant
Assigning administrative unit membership
explanation: Internet Access is Microsoft's identity-aware Secure Web Gateway component, applying policy-based filtering and protection to general internet and SaaS-bound traffic. It's unrelated to AD replication (B), custom domain configuration (C), or administrative unit membership (D).

question: An organization specifically wants optimized, secured, and identity-aware routing for Microsoft 365 traffic (Teams, Exchange Online, SharePoint) through Global Secure Access. What should they deploy?
options: Internet Access for Microsoft 365, a purpose-built profile optimized for M365 traffic within Global Secure Access
Private Access only, since M365 is technically a private resource
A completely separate third-party SWG product, since Entra doesn't support this
Company branding customization
explanation: Global Secure Access includes an Internet Access profile specifically tuned for Microsoft 365 traffic, balancing performance and security for that traffic class. M365 is a cloud SaaS service, not a private/on-prem resource, so Private Access (B) is the wrong fit, Entra does support this natively so C is false, and branding (D) is irrelevant.

question: What is a 'break-glass' or emergency access account used for in the context of Conditional Access planning?
options: A shared account with no password, used by all employees for convenience
A tightly controlled, highly monitored account excluded from restrictive Conditional Access policies, reserved for use only if normal admin access is unexpectedly locked out
A guest account for external vendors
An account automatically created for every new hire
explanation: Break-glass accounts are a deliberate safety valve — excluded from CA policies and heavily monitored/alerted on any use — so a policy misconfiguration or MFA outage can't permanently lock administrators out of their own tenant. It's not a shared convenience account (A), not for vendors (C), and not something auto-created per new hire (D).

question: A Conditional Access policy uses grant controls set to 'Require one of the selected controls' with both 'Require MFA' and 'Require compliant device' selected. What is required for access?
options: Both MFA and compliant device are mandatory together
Satisfying just one of the two — either MFA or a compliant device — is sufficient
Neither control is enforced under 'require one'
Only compliant device satisfies the policy; MFA is ignored
explanation: 'Require one of the selected controls' is an OR condition — satisfying any single selected control is enough to be granted access, unlike 'require all' which needs every control satisfied. Both being mandatory (A) describes the AND logic instead, and neither being enforced (C) or MFA being ignored outright (D) are incorrect.

question: Which PowerShell/Graph capability would an admin use to immediately revoke all of a specific user's currently active refresh tokens across all their signed-in sessions?
options: Revoke-MgUserSignInSession (or the equivalent 'Revoke sessions' action in the portal)
Update-MgUserLicense
New-MgGroup
Set-MgDomain
explanation: Revoking sign-in sessions invalidates a user's refresh tokens tenant-wide, forcing re-authentication everywhere. License updates (B), group creation (C), and domain configuration (D) have no bearing on active session/token state.

question: A global admin adds 'ContosoFall2026' to the custom banned password list. What is the practical effect?
options: Users can no longer use any password containing that string or close fuzzy-matching variants of it, whether on cloud or (if the on-prem proxy/agent is deployed) on-premises password changes
The string is only blocked for the Global Administrator's own account
The banned list has no effect until the tenant is upgraded to a higher license tier
The password immediately becomes the required password for all new accounts
explanation: Custom banned list entries are checked (with fuzzy matching for common substitutions) against any password set by any in-scope user, cloud or on-prem (if the proxy is deployed) — it's not scoped to just the admin who added it (B), doesn't require a specific extra license tier beyond what's already needed for the feature (C), and doesn't set any password as required (D, which misunderstands what a banned list does).

question: What is the difference between 'Security defaults' and a custom Conditional Access-based MFA policy?
options: They are functionally and configurably identical

Security defaults are a simple, free, one-size-fits-all baseline (e.g., requiring MFA for all users) with minimal customization, while Conditional Access policies allow granular, tenant-specific rules (per app, per group, per risk level, etc.) but typically require an Entra ID P1/P2 license
Security defaults require a P2 license, while Conditional Access is always free
Security defaults can only be enabled after Conditional Access is fully configured
explanation: Security defaults are Microsoft's straightforward, broadly-applied baseline protection intended for organizations without premium licensing, while Conditional Access offers much finer-grained control but generally needs Entra ID P1 or higher. The licensing direction in C is reversed, and they aren't identical (A) or sequentially dependent as described in D.

question: Which of the following is a real-time event that Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) is designed to react to almost immediately, rather than waiting for token expiry?
options: A scheduled quarterly access review completing
A user account being disabled by an admin
A company branding logo update
A new custom security attribute definition being created
explanation: CAE reacts to critical events like account disablement, password reset, or detected high user risk by prompting near-real-time re-evaluation/revocation for CAE-aware services. Access review completion (A), branding updates (C), and attribute definition creation (D) aren't the kind of critical security events CAE is built to react to instantly.

question: An Azure Function needs to read secrets from Azure Key Vault at runtime with no credentials stored in code or config. What identity type is the best-practice choice?
options: A shared user account with a hardcoded password in the function's app settings
A system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity, which Azure automatically manages credentials for with no secrets to store
A service principal with a manually created, long-lived client secret stored in a config file
A personal Global Administrator account used by the developer
explanation: Managed identities are Azure's purpose-built solution for exactly this scenario — Azure handles credential issuance/rotation automatically, eliminating stored secrets entirely. A hardcoded password (A) and a manually stored client secret (C) both create secret-management risk, and using a personal admin account (D) is a severe security anti-pattern mixing human and workload identity.

question: What is the key difference between a system-assigned and a user-assigned managed identity?
options: There is no difference, they behave identically in all cases

A system-assigned identity's lifecycle is tied directly to the single Azure resource it's created for (deleted when the resource is deleted), while a user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that can be assigned to multiple Azure resources and outlives any one of them
User-assigned identities can only be used with virtual machines
System-assigned identities can be shared across resources, while user-assigned identities cannot
explanation: System-assigned identities live and die with their host resource, while user-assigned identities are independently managed and can be attached to multiple resources — the reverse of what option D claims. They aren't identical (A), and user-assigned identities work with many resource types, not just VMs (C).

question: An application runs outside of Azure (e.g., on-premises or in another cloud) but needs to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID to call Microsoft Graph. Since managed identities are Azure-resource-bound, what identity should be used instead?
options: A service principal (app registration) with its own credential — a certificate or client secret — used in a client-credentials OAuth flow
A managed identity forced onto the external server
A personal user account shared by the app
No identity is needed if the app only reads public data
explanation: Managed identities require an Azure-hosted resource to attach to, so workloads outside Azure use a standard app registration/service principal authenticating with a certificate or secret via the client-credentials flow. Managed identity can't be 'forced' onto non-Azure infrastructure (B), sharing a personal account for an app is a security anti-pattern (C), and calling Graph still requires an authenticated identity even for reads (D).

question: How does an admin create a system-assigned managed identity for an Azure App Service?
options: By manually registering an app in Microsoft Entra ID and copying its client secret into the App Service
By enabling the 'System assigned' managed identity toggle directly on the App Service resource, which causes Azure to automatically create and manage the underlying service principal
Managed identities cannot be created for App Service, only for virtual machines
By assigning an Entra role to the App Service's resource group
explanation: System-assigned managed identities are enabled with a simple toggle directly on the supporting resource (like App Service); Azure creates and lifecycle-manages the backing service principal automatically — no manual app registration or secret copying is involved (A is false), App Service is one of many supported resource types beyond VMs (C is false), and role assignment to a resource group is a separate downstream step, not identity creation itself (D).

question: After creating a user-assigned managed identity, what additional step is required before a virtual machine can actually use it?
options: Nothing further — creation automatically attaches it to every VM in the subscription
The user-assigned identity must be explicitly assigned/attached to the specific VM resource
The VM must be restarted with a new OS image
The identity must be manually entered as a login credential inside the VM's OS
explanation: A user-assigned managed identity exists as an independent resource and must be explicitly attached to each VM (or other resource) that should use it — it doesn't auto-attach tenant-wide (A is false), doesn't require a VM restart with a new image (C is false), and isn't used as an in-OS login credential (D is false — it's used via the Azure Instance Metadata Service endpoint).

question: A VM with a managed identity needs to read blobs from an Azure Storage account. Besides having the managed identity attached to the VM, what else must be configured?
options: Nothing else — attaching the identity automatically grants access to every Azure resource in the tenant
An appropriate Azure RBAC role assignment (e.g., Storage Blob Data Reader) granting the managed identity's principal permission on the storage account
A Conditional Access policy targeting the storage account
A custom security attribute on the storage account
explanation: Managed identities still need explicit Azure RBAC role assignments on the target resource to actually have permission — attaching the identity alone grants no access anywhere (A is false). Conditional Access (C) governs interactive user sign-in scenarios, not this kind of resource-to-resource Azure RBAC authorization, and custom security attributes (D) don't grant data-plane permissions.

question: What is the typical mechanism an application code uses to actually retrieve a token for its managed identity at runtime?
options: The developer manually copies a token from the Azure portal into the app's config file

The app calls the local Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) endpoint (or uses an SDK like Azure.Identity's DefaultAzureCredential/ManagedIdentityCredential), which handles token acquisition and caching transparently
The app prompts the end user to sign in interactively
The app reads the token from a plaintext file checked into source control
explanation: Managed identity token acquisition happens automatically through the local metadata endpoint (or an SDK credential class wrapping it) — no manual copying (A), no interactive user prompt (C, since this is a non-interactive workload identity), and certainly no plaintext token in source control (D, which would defeat the entire purpose of avoiding stored secrets).

question: What is a managed service account, and how does it differ from a managed identity in Microsoft Entra ID?
options: They are the exact same concept with different names

A managed service account (e.g., a Group Managed Service Account, gMSA) is an on-premises Active Directory construct for automatic password management of service accounts running Windows services; a Microsoft Entra managed identity is a cloud-native Azure resource identity — they solve a similar 'no manual credential management' goal but in different environments
Managed service accounts only exist in Microsoft Entra ID, never in on-premises AD
Managed identities require a service account to be created first in AD
explanation: gMSAs are a long-standing on-prem AD feature for automatic credential rotation of Windows service accounts, conceptually similar in goal to managed identities but implemented entirely differently in a different environment — they are not the same construct (A is false), gMSAs originate in on-prem AD, not Entra ID (C is false), and Entra managed identities have no dependency on an AD service account existing first (D is false).

question: What is the difference between application-level and tenant-level settings for an enterprise application in Microsoft Entra ID?
options: There is no distinction; all settings apply identically everywhere

Application-level settings (like sign-in behavior, user assignment requirement, and app roles) apply only to that specific application, while tenant-level settings (like whether users can consent to apps at all) apply organization-wide across all applications
Tenant-level settings can only be configured by the application's original developer
Application-level settings always override tenant-level settings, even security-restrictive ones
explanation: Application-level configuration scopes to one specific enterprise app, while tenant-level settings (like the user consent policy) act as an organization-wide governance layer — real distinction exists (A is false). Tenant-level settings aren't developer-restricted (C is false, they're an Entra admin capability) and app-level settings can't simply override a tenant-wide restrictive consent policy (D is false).

question: Which built-in Microsoft Entra role is scoped specifically to managing enterprise application registrations and their assignments, without full Global Administrator rights?
options: Application Administrator (or the more limited Cloud Application Administrator)
Billing Administrator
Compliance Administrator
Exchange Administrator
explanation: Application Administrator (and its Cloud Application Administrator variant, which excludes on-prem app proxy management) is purpose-built for managing app registrations and enterprise app configuration without granting broader Global Administrator rights. Billing (B), Compliance (C), and Exchange (D) Administrator roles are scoped to entirely different areas.

question: An organization wants remote employees to securely access an internal, on-premises web application without a traditional VPN, using their existing Entra ID sign-in. What should they configure?
options: Microsoft Entra Application Proxy, publishing the on-prem app with a lightweight connector installed on-premises
A brand-new SaaS rewrite of the application
A Conditional Access named location covering all remote IP ranges
A user-assigned managed identity attached to the on-prem server
explanation: Application Proxy is specifically designed to expose on-premises web apps externally through Entra ID authentication via a lightweight connector, without requiring a full VPN or app rewrite. Rewriting the app as SaaS (B) isn't necessary or implied by the requirement, named locations alone (C) don't provide the actual proxy/publishing mechanism, and managed identities (D) are for Azure workload authentication, not remote user access to on-prem apps.

question: What is generally the fastest way to integrate a well-known SaaS application (e.g., a popular CRM) with Microsoft Entra ID for SSO and provisioning?
options: Always build a custom SAML app registration from scratch, even if the app is already in the gallery
Search the Microsoft Entra application gallery for the pre-integrated SaaS app, which typically includes pre-configured SSO and, where supported, automated SCIM provisioning
Use Microsoft Entra Application Proxy, since it's the only way to connect any external app
Manually recreate every SaaS user as a separate Entra guest account with no federation
explanation: The application gallery contains thousands of pre-integrated apps with ready-made SSO configuration templates and often SCIM-based automatic provisioning, dramatically speeding up integration versus building from scratch (A) unnecessarily. Application Proxy (C) is specifically for on-prem apps, not the general SaaS integration method, and manually recreating disconnected guest accounts (D) defeats the purpose of federated SSO.

question: An enterprise app has 'User assignment required' set to Yes. What is the effect on who can access it?
options: Any authenticated tenant user can access the app regardless of assignment
Only users (or members of groups) explicitly assigned to the app can access it — unassigned users are blocked even if they'd otherwise be able to authenticate
This setting only affects the app's icon visibility on the My Apps portal, not actual access
It disables Conditional Access for that app
explanation: 'User assignment required' enforces that only explicitly assigned users/groups can actually access the app, providing an authorization gate beyond mere authentication — it doesn't just affect portal icon visibility (C is false, that's a cosmetic side effect at most) and has no bearing on Conditional Access applicability (D is false). Without this setting enabled, any authenticated user in the tenant generally could access it, which is the opposite of A being the effect when the setting IS enabled.

question: What are app roles used for when assigning users or groups to an enterprise application?
options: App roles let the application receive information about what level of access/permission the assigned user or group should have inside the app itself (e.g., 'Reader' vs 'Admin'), via a claim in the issued token
App roles control the tenant's Company branding for that app
App roles are only used for licensing purposes, unrelated to authorization
App roles replace the need for Conditional Access policies on that app
explanation: App roles are defined by the app (in its manifest/registration) and assigned to users/groups, then surfaced as a roles claim in the token so the app itself can make in-app authorization decisions. They have no relationship to branding (B), aren't purely a licensing concept (C), and don't substitute for Conditional Access (D, which governs access conditions rather than in-app authorization).

question: What is the difference between user consent and admin consent for an application requesting API permissions?
options: They are identical; both require the same approval process

User consent lets an individual user approve permissions on their own behalf (often limited to lower-risk, non-admin-consent-required permissions); admin consent is granted by an administrator on behalf of the entire organization (or specific users/groups), often required for higher-privilege permissions
User consent always applies organization-wide automatically
Admin consent can only be granted by the app's original developer
